html:
The Free City of Lübeck was a self-ruling city-state on the Baltic coast of northern Germany, near the mouth of the Trave. It is on the map for 1715.

Henry the Lion, Duke of Saxony, refounded the town in 1159, and in 1226 the emperor made it a free imperial city, answering only to him. Lübeck became the leading town of the Hanseatic League, the trading network that ran Baltic and North Sea commerce for three centuries, and its town law was copied by about a hundred towns around the Baltic.

By 1715 the Hansa had faded and Lübeck was a modest merchant city, though still free inside the Holy Roman Empire. It kept that status as a state of Germany until 1937, when the Nazi government merged it into Prussia. Its neighbours were Mecklenburg and the duchies held by Denmark.
